text: Four lessons, one company, and seven chapters of this course all pulling together. Caldwell Logistics synced its identity, encrypted its data, managed its secrets, caught a real misconfiguration, and fixed it — and this review walks back through why each earlier chapter is what made that possible.

Chapter 1 argued that hybrid identity exists because a company can't just abandon decades of on-prem Active Directory, and that password hash sync keeps the resulting failure domain small — exactly why Lesson 29 chose it over federation. Chapter 2's Zero Trust principle, that identity is the new perimeter evaluated continuously rather than trusted once, is why Lesson 29 didn't stop at a completed sync. It kept going until Conditional Access actually fired against the new accounts.

Chapters 3 and 4 are related but genuinely different problems, and Lesson 30 used both without blurring them. The customer-managed key protecting Caldwell's storage account is Chapter 3's subject — who controls the key, rotated automatically by Key Vault with no human involved. The database connection string moved into Key Vault is Chapter 4's subject — a credential that never belonged in a config file, rotated only once a Function actually does the work.

Chapter 5's CSPM concepts are exactly what caught Lesson 31's real public-access finding, traced it to a genuine root cause in the Activity Log, and confirmed the fix by re-scanning instead of assuming it worked. Chapter 6 never got its own capstone lab, but it's the quiet precondition underneath both of Lesson 30's and Lesson 31's work — Caldwell's team manages its Key Vault and storage account over a site-to-site VPN, never an admin endpoint exposed to the open internet.

Chapter 7 taught the shared responsibility model and frameworks like SOC 2 on their own, but by this chapter it had already become the thread running through the other three lessons. The customer-managed key exists because compliance wanted provable control over key lifecycle. The CSPM finding matters to an auditor because an unremediated public-access flag is exactly what shows up on a SOC 2 report. Every other chapter's work only counts once it's provable, not just true.

That's the full course — from why hybrid identity exists to deploying it, encrypting data and managing secrets end to end, catching and fixing a real posture-management finding, and tying all seven chapters into one secured, watched, auditable environment. Next up in this path: PowerShell, Python, Azure CLI & Infrastructure Automation.
